note.note:
History:
- Chief complaint: Difficulty breathing after insect sting (bee/wasp uncertain) with local rash on arm; subjective mild right-sided lip swelling and “weird” tongue sensation.
- Onset/duration: Sting occurred minutes before the consult; symptoms present at time of call.
- Course/severity: Breathing not “particularly acute” per patient; anxiety present; seeking reassurance. No prior anaphylaxis; never had an EpiPen.
- Context: Sting to arm; localized redness with puncture mark. No medications taken yet for this episode.

Past Medical History:
- Eczema.
- Occasional anxiety/panic attacks.
- Allergies: Penicillin.
- Medications: None taken for this episode; chronic/home meds not documented.
- Family history: No relevant acute reactions reported.
- Social: Works as a computer scientist; lives alone; has a cat. No known pet allergies.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- General/respiratory: Speaking comfortably; breathing appeared normal on video per clinician; no observed stridor.
- Oropharynx/lips: No visible lip swelling; oropharyngeal view unremarkable on video. Patient reports tongue feels “weird.”
- Skin (arm): Slight localized redness/blotchiness at sting site with a puncture mark; no notable swelling seen.
- Neurologic/mental status: Not specifically documented.

Impression:
- Localized allergic/inflammatory reaction to Hymenoptera sting with associated anxiety; no objective airway compromise on exam.
- DDx (consistent with transcript):
  - Localized allergic/inflammatory reaction to sting: Most likely; localized erythema, stable exam.
  - Early anaphylaxis: Possible given temporal link and subjective oral sensations; no objective findings during visit.
  - Anxiety-related dyspnea: Possible contributor given normal observed breathing and history of panic.

Management Plan:
- Medications: Start an over-the-counter antihistamine.
  - Chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet, up to six times daily.
  - Alternatively, a once-daily antihistamine (one-a-day), per patient preference. Dose/brand not specified.
- Education and red flags: If any breathing difficulty, lip/tongue swelling, stridor, or voice change develops—or if symptoms rapidly worsen—go to the emergency department (ED) immediately.
- Local wound care/monitoring: Observe the arm. If redness spreads, becomes hot, or signs of local infection appear, seek care; antibiotics may be considered at that time.
- Testing/referrals: No allergy testing indicated now; consider if reactions become recurrent or if other non-specific rashes occur.
- Information provided: Link to anaphylaxis education for awareness of warning signs.
- Follow-up: Contact the clinic for any change in symptoms or if reassurance is needed.

Patient Summary:
- A 27-year-old man was stung on the arm minutes before the visit and reported anxiety, subjective mild oral swelling, and perceived breathing difficulty. Video assessment showed normal breathing, no visible lip/oropharyngeal swelling, and a localized skin reaction at the sting site.
- Impression favors a localized reaction with anxiety; advised OTC antihistamines, monitoring, and strict return/ED precautions for any airway symptoms or rapid progression.

Key Takeaways:
- Begin antihistamine as advised; a chlorphenamine option is 4 mg up to six times daily or a once-daily alternative.
- Seek urgent care immediately if breathing worsens, lips/tongue swell, or stridor/voice changes occur.
- Monitor the sting site; seek care if redness spreads or the area becomes hot/tender.

Next Steps:
- Start antihistamine today and observe over the next 24–48 hours.
- If symptoms recur in future stings or rashes, discuss potential allergy testing with primary care.
- No tests or prescriptions were issued today.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Vitals, complete medication list, past surgical history, immunizations, tobacco/alcohol/substance use, full review of systems, height/weight.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted; both support localized reaction with caution for early anaphylaxis.
- Transcript quality: Some hesitations/pauses; key history and exam details are adequately captured.
